paper_metadata.title: Tailoring FCC-Ti(N) precipitates in kilogram-scale TiVNb-N alloys for enhanced intermediate-temperature performance
paper_metadata.journal: International Journal of Refractory Metals and Hard Materials

evidence.quote: A 4 kg nitrogen-doped (1 at.%) TiVNb lightweight medium-entropy alloy (MEA) was fabricated by vacuum magnetic suspension melting for high-temperature applications.

The observed hardness increase in the bottom region correlates strongly with the near-absence of precipitates, suggesting that solid solution strengthening becomes the dominant hardening mechanism in this zone.

After heat treatment at 600 ◦C for 8 h, the alloy exhibits significantly improved microstructural homogeneity, with the nitrogen content in the FCC-Ti(N) phase increasing by over 20 at.%. This leads to remarkable enhancements in both strength and ductility.

evidence.section: 3.2.2. The stability and effect of FCC-Ti phase
evidence.quote: It indicates a strong pinning effect exerted by FCC-Ti precipitates at the GBs, which effectively resists GB migration during deformation.

evidence.section: 3.2.2. The stability and effect of FCC-Ti phase
evidence.quote: At RT, dislocation slip and accumulation at matrix GBs restrict the motion of FCC-Ti phases, primarily manifesting as sliding deformation.

evidence.section: 3.2.2. The stability and effect of FCC-Ti phase
evidence.quote: Whereas at elevated temperatures, accelerated dynamic recovery reduces stress concentration at GBs of BCC matrix, allowing FCC-Ti grains to rotate during matrix flow deformation, thereby increasing intergranular orientation discrepancies.
The increased amount of FCC-Ti(N) precipitates, accompanied by increased nitrogen solubility within these precipitates, enhances the strengthening effect of the second phase.
Meanwhile, the finely dispersed precipitates hinder dislocation motion more effectively.
